confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Roberts, David. 2022. Moraic tone-bearing units in Kabiye. Linguistique et Langues Africaines 8(1): 1-35. DOI 10.4000/lla.2154 (open access, journals.openedition.org/lla/2154)
catalog_locator: p. 26, section 5.2 'Post-lexical HLH plateauing' (OpenEdition HTML para. 63); tone statement p. 5, section 2.2 'Tones'; footnote 4, p. 7, attached to section 3.2 'Defining the syllable' ('below the level of the prosodic word').
catalog_quote: Admittedly, since a moraic account prohibits downstep occurring between two moras with no intervening consonant, one might legitimately ask why weightless consonant onsets should participate in the placement of downstep. The usual evidence for this comes from stress assignment patterns, where the presence of a consonant onset causes a syllable to attract stress, but this is not the case in Kabiye phonology because stress is not phonemic. ... Now let us turn to the tone system. Kabiye has two underlying tones, H and L (Lébikaza 1999: 183) and — assuming that the OCP is inoperative (Roberts 2016: 148) — eight underlying tone patterns on non-compound nouns (4). ... [fn. 4] In some languages with phonemic stress, it may be necessary to state “below the level of the foot”, but this is not the case in Kabiye.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kabiyé is a two-tone language (H, L; Roberts 2022 p. 1 citing Lébikaza 1999: 183). Stress is stated to be non-phonemic; no position for word stress is described anywhere in the accessible literature, and the tonal literature (Roberts 2003, 2008, 2019, 2021, 2022) never invokes stress or prominence as a factor. No fixed or predictable stress position can be assigned from the sources read.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source read.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is a passing remark inside an argument about moraic tone-bearing units, not a dedicated stress section.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology (tone assignment to moras/syllables in nouns and verbs); the remark concerns phonemic (contrastive) stress, and says nothing about phonetic prominence in citation forms or phrases.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Kabiyé proper (kbp, kabi1261) as spoken in the Kara region of Togo; Roberts' data are from his own fieldwork with L1 speakers; no dialect specified beyond the standard variety used for the orthography. The earlier scan's named source 'Roberts 2011, Grammaire kabiyè: une esquisse (SIL)' could not be confirmed to exist.

Kabiye contrasts only two level tones: the /H/ tone and the /L/ tone, which manifest themselves in the word as [H], [L], and a downstepped high tone". p. 162: Lébikaza (1985, 1989, 1999) correlates root-initial obstruent voicing "to an 'interaction between segmental and suprasegmental features,' i.e., tone, syllable length, and stress."

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog record (Kabiye, no stress rule) and with Roberts 2022 ('stress is not phonemic'): Padayodi treats Kabiye as a two-tone language and offers no stress placement. It adds a pointer that Lébikaza 1999 (print only, pp. 135-142 and a prosody section) does discuss an 'accent'/stress notion, which no open source read so far describes.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kabiye is analysed as a two-tone (H, L) language with downstep and HL/LH contours on CVV syllables; the dissertation explicitly excludes accent (stress) and intonation from its scope and makes no claim of its own about where word stress falls or whether it exists. It only reports second-hand that Lébikaza (1999: 135-142) invokes 'stress' alongside tone and syllable length in accounting for obstruent voicing, and (p. 17) that Lébikaza 1999 has a section on 'accent, pause, and intonation'; footnote 30 (p. 107) quotes Delord 1976 warning that Europeans tend to hear the high-toned syllable as the accented one.
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; only tonal matters (contours restricted to CVV syllables, downstep).
new_statements.identity_note: Padayodi describes standard Kabiye (Kɛ̀wɛ-based variety, Togo); she notes Delord 1976 data partly reflect the Lɪkpá and Lá'máɖɪ́sɪ varieties. No dialect difference bearing on stress is reported.

tone_statements.citation: Roberts, David & Stephen L. Walter. 2012. Writing grammar rather than tone: An orthography experiment in Togo. Written Language & Literacy 15(2): 226-253. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. DOI 10.1075/wll.15.2.06rob.
tone_statements.quote: Kabiye has two phonemic tones, high (H) and low (L), automatic and non-automatic downstep and numerous morphotonological processes that have been described in detail elsewhere (Delord 1976; Kassan 2000; Lébikaza 1994; Lébikaza 1999; Roberts 2002, 2003a, 2003b). Although tone plays a lexical and a grammatical role, all our previous research indicates that the real functional load of tone is in the grammar (Roberts 2008a, 2010a, 2010b). Indeed numerous grammatical constructions are signaled only by tone. However, the Standard Orthography does not mark tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.1 'The kabiyè language', prepublication p. 6, just after Table 3
tone_statements.summary: Two phonemic level tones, high and low, with automatic and non-automatic downstep; tone is lexical and grammatical, many grammatical constructions signalled by tone alone. Nothing on word stress.

tone_statements.summary: Two underlying tones H and L; six lexical melodies on nouns (H, L, HL, LH, HLH, LHL) linked to the word; moraic TBU incl. some nasals; L spread, HLH plateauing, H spread; non-automatic (phonemic) downstep from floating L.

tone_statements.citation: Roberts, David. 2010. Exploring written ambiguities can help assess where to mark tone. Writing Systems Research 2(1): 25-40. DOI 10.1093/wsr/wsq003.
tone_statements.quote: The Kabiye tone system is characterized by two discrete level tones, H and L, automatic and non-automatic downstep. Numerous lexical and post-lexical morphotonological processes occur once words are placed in context (Delord, 1976; Kassan, 2000; Lébikaza, 2003; Lébikaza, 1994; Lébikaza, 1999; Roberts, 2002, 2003a, 2003b). Although tone plays an important role in both the lexicon and the grammar, it is in the latter that it bears the greater burden.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.4 'A response to felt needs', manuscript p. 5 (journal pp. 25-40 not in this copy); /HLH/ downstep rule, ex. 34-39 and floating L triggering non-automatic downstep in sec. 3.2, ms p. 12.
tone_statements.summary: Two discrete level tones, H and L, with automatic and non-automatic downstep; a floating low tone left by elision triggers downstep; many morphotonological processes; word stress not discussed.

tone_statements.citation: Padayodi, Cécile M. 2008. Kabiye. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 38(2): 215-221 (Illustrations of the IPA). DOI 10.1017/S0025100308003496.
tone_statements.quote: Prosodic features Two distinctive tone levels are recognized in Kabiye: high /ˊ/ and low /ˋ/. The language also exhibits a downstepped variant of the high tone [ ↓ ˊ]. Syllabic nasals [m] and [ŋ] and vowels are the Tone Bearing Units with long vowels appearing to allow for the presence of limited tonal contours. It is also important to mention that the tone phenomena variously termed ‘declination’, ‘downstep’, and ‘downdrift’ in the literature are very apparent. Likewise, the process of tone spread is very common. To date, there has not been any solid study of these phenomena, so the very complex tonal processes of the language are not well understood.
tone_statements.locator: section 'Prosodic features' (pp. 215-221, paragraph preceding 'Transcription of recorded passage')
tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones H/L + downstepped H; TBU = vowel (mora-like: long vowels carry contours) and syllabic nasal; downdrift and tone spreading; tone unmarked in standard orthography.

tone_statements.citation: Roberts, David. 2010. Vers une graphie tonale appropriée pour le kabiyè : une troisième voie. Papers presented at the extraordinary meeting of the Comité de Langue Nationale Kabiyè, Lomé, Togo, 28 June - 1 July 2010. PDF (213 KB) distributed on the author's website (nyiniyu.com, 'Orthography reports'). [Announced in Roberts 2008: 595 as 'Pour une troisième voie dans la graphie tonale des langues africaines: le cas du kabiyè', à paraître in Grand'Eury-Buron & Diki-Kidiri (eds.), LLACAN - that chapter never appeared.]
tone_statements.quote: Le fait que l’écrasante majorité des langues africaines sont des langues à tons a suscité un vif débat sur la question de la représentation du ton à l’écrit. … Le kabiyè n'échappe pas au débat. L'orthographe standard ne marque pas les tons, … Deux des pronoms sujets sont des paires minimales de ton. … il s'agit du pronom sujet [ a ~ á ] ils ~ elles, prononcé soit avec un ton B soit avec un ton H en fonction de la conjugaison, et pour les deux derniers il s'agit du pronom interrogatif [ á ] qui ? prononcé à ton H.
tone_statements.translation: The fact that the overwhelming majority of African languages are tone languages has provoked lively debate on the representation of tone in writing. … Kabiye does not escape the debate. The standard orthography does not mark tones, … Two of the subject pronouns are tonal minimal pairs. … it is the subject pronoun [ a ~ á ] 'they', pronounced either with a L tone or with a H tone depending on the conjugation, and for the last two it is the interrogative pronoun [ á ] 'who?' pronounced with H tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1 Préambule p. 5, sec. 2 p. 6, and sec. 4.3 p. 19
tone_statements.summary: Tone language with high (H) and low (B) tones named in passing on pronouns and verb prefixes; tonal minimal pairs among subject pronouns; tone unmarked in standard orthography; no inventory stated.

tone.translation: The fact that the overwhelming majority of African languages are tone languages has provoked lively debate on the representation of tone in writing. … Kabiye does not escape the debate. The standard orthography does not mark tones, … Two of the subject pronouns are tonal minimal pairs. … it is the subject pronoun [ a ~ á ] 'they', pronounced either with a L tone or with a H tone depending on the conjugation, and for the last two it is the interrogative pronoun [ á ] 'who?' pronounced with H tone.
tone.summary: Tone language with high (H) and low (B) tones named in passing on pronouns and verb prefixes; tonal minimal pairs among subject pronouns; tone unmarked in standard orthography; no inventory stated.
